title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Objectives

Understand the role of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in ensuring safety in the National Airspace System (NAS)
Recognize the main types of UAS operations and distinguish between them
Name the requirements for legal commercial UAS operations in the U.S., both for the pilot and for the UAS
Outline the requirements for recreational flying under the 49 USC 44809 exception, including TRUST


Frame the lecture: last week was what UAS are; this week is when and how you may legally fly them. Emphasize that everyone in the room who ever launches a drone, even a 249 g toy in a park, falls under one of these rule sets. The recreational exception is a statute (49 USC 44809, from the 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act), while commercial rules are regulation (14 CFR Part 107, effective August 29, 2016).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Objectives

Know the operating rules for commercial use of UAS (Part 107)
Understand how airspace authorization works today (LAANC) and recognize permanent and temporary “no-drone-zones”
Understand the role of the Certificate of Authorization (COA) for public agencies
Recognize when educational use of UAS falls under the recreational exception and when it requires Part 107


Point out that this material changes often: the rules taught in this course in 2017 are substantially different from today’s. Encourage students to always verify against faa.gov/uas rather than blog posts. Mapping work done for the university or a client is commercial in the FAA’s eyes, so Part 107 is the rule set most relevant to this course.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)



Created in 1958 in response to a series of fatal accidents and midair collisions involving commercial aircraft
Mandated to develop plans and policies for the use of navigable airspace to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace
Since the creation of the FAA, American airspace has become one of the most regulated fields in the United States





The 1956 Grand Canyon midair collision is the classic trigger event; the Federal Aviation Act of 1958 created the agency. The key takeaway for drone pilots: the FAA owns the airspace from the ground up. There is no unregulated altitude band below 400 ft; that figure is an operating limit, not a boundary of FAA authority.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
National Airspace System (NAS)

Already congested with piloted aircraft, and adding a swarm of UAS requires thoughtful planning
Main mandate: to ensure that UAS do not endanger current users of the NAS nor compromise the safety of people and property on the ground 


Detect-and-avoid is the drone equivalent of “see and avoid” that manned pilots perform visually. Because a remote pilot cannot scan the sky from the cockpit, the default mitigations are visual line of sight and yielding right of way. This is the thread that connects most Part 107 operating rules, and the reason beyond-visual-line-of-sight flight currently requires a waiver. Foreshadow the Part 108 slide at the end.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Types of UAS operations



Commercial / civil: any flight in furtherance of a business or non-recreational purpose, under 14 CFR Part 107
Recreational: strictly for personal enjoyment, under the 49 USC 44809 exception
Public aircraft operations: government entities, under Part 107 or a Certificate of Authorization (COA)
Educational use can fall under the recreational exception or Part 107, depending on the activity





The 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act repealed the old “model aircraft” rule (Section 336) and replaced it with the 44809 recreational exception; the FAA no longer uses “model aircraft” as an operational category. Stress that intent, not the aircraft, determines the category: the same Mini 4 Pro is recreational in a park on Saturday and commercial when photographing a field site for a project.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use of UAS



Operation of an unmanned aircraft strictly for personal interests and enjoyment
Taking photographs for your own personal use is recreational
Taking the same photographs for compensation, for sale, or in furtherance of any business (including research or coursework deliverables for pay) is a commercial operation under Part 107





Useful test question for the class: is posting drone footage to a monetized YouTube channel recreational? (No; compensation makes it commercial.) Is flying to practice piloting skills for a future Part 107 job recreational? (FAA guidance says yes, if the flight itself is purely for enjoyment/proficiency.) The line is the purpose of the individual flight.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use - the 44809 exception
To fly recreationally without a Part 107 certificate you must follow all conditions of 49 USC 44809:



Fly strictly for recreational purposes
Pass TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test) and carry proof of completion
Register the aircraft if it weighs 250 g or more (FAADroneZone) and comply with Remote ID
Follow the safety guidelines of an FAA-recognized Community Based Organization (CBO)





TRUST (required since 2021) is free, online, cannot be failed (wrong answers are corrected and re-asked), and takes about 30 minutes; proof must be shown to the FAA or law enforcement on request. Recognized CBOs include the Academy of Model Aeronautics and FPV Freedom Coalition; their published guidelines fill in operational detail the statute leaves open. Registration is $5 for 3 years and the number goes on the aircraft.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use - the 44809 exception



Keep the aircraft within visual line of sight (or use a co-located visual observer)
Give way to and never interfere with manned aircraft
Fly at or below 400 ft in uncontrolled (Class G) airspace
In controlled airspace (Class B, C, D, E surface areas): fly only with a LAANC authorization or FAA authorization, at or below the UAS Facility Map altitude





This slide is where the old rules differ most from current ones: the pre-2019 “notify airports within 5 miles” requirement is gone. Today recreational and commercial pilots use the same LAANC system for controlled-airspace authorization, covered in detail later in this lecture. UAS Facility Maps grid the airspace around airports into maximum authorized altitudes (often 0 ft near the runway ends).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use - safety practices



Ensure the operating environment is safe and the operator is competent and proficient
Do not fly over people or moving vehicles, and keep a safe distance from individuals and vulnerable property
Do not fly near or over sensitive infrastructure (power stations, water treatment facilities, correctional facilities, heavily traveled roadways, government facilities)
Do not fly in adverse weather such as high winds or reduced visibility





These practices come from the CBO safety guidelines that the statute requires recreational flyers to follow. They mirror many Part 107 rules, which makes the later transition to certificated flying easier. Wind is the practical one for mapping students: most small quads struggle above roughly 20 mph sustained wind, well before the flight becomes illegal it becomes useless for data quality.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use - safety practices



Check and follow all local laws and ordinances before flying over private property
Do not conduct surveillance or photograph persons where there is an expectation of privacy without permission
Do not fly under the influence of alcohol or drugs





Privacy is mostly governed by state and local law, not the FAA. North Carolina’s drone statutes (G.S. 15A-300.1) prohibit surveillance of persons or private property without consent, with civil damages available. Good discussion prompt: who enforces what? The FAA handles airspace violations; local police handle privacy, trespass, and harassment complaints.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use of UAS
Any use in connection with a business or work, including:



Selling photos or videos taken from a UAS
Providing contract services, such as industrial equipment or factory inspection
Providing professional services, such as security or telecommunications
Monitoring the progress of work your company is performing
University research and mapping projects like the ones in this course


 


The FAA interprets “commercial” broadly: any flight in furtherance of a business or performed as part of one’s job, whether or not money changes hands for the flight itself. Faculty research flights and most university data-collection missions are Part 107 operations. This is why the flight operations later in this course are conducted under Part 107 by certificated pilots.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - Remote Pilot requirements

Must be at least 16 years of age
Be able to read, speak, write, and understand English
Be in a physical and mental condition to safely fly a drone
Pass the initial aeronautical knowledge exam: “Unmanned Aircraft General - Small (UAG)”




Must pass the applicable Transportation Security Administration (TSA) vetting
See the course Step-by-Step Guide to Getting an FAA Part 107 License





The knowledge test is 60 multiple-choice questions, 2 hours, 70% to pass, about $175 at a PSI testing center. Point students to the step-by-step guide on the course site; also note the certificate is not required for this course, but it is one of the most employable single credentials a geospatial student can add. Assignment 1B has them work through sample test questions.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Remote Pilot Certificate


Requirements

Must be easily accessible by the remote pilot during all UAS operations
Certificate holders must complete free online recurrent training every 24 calendar months to maintain aeronautical knowledge recency (effective April 2021)
FAA Safety Team Part 107 Small UAS Training Course (login required)





Before April 2021 keeping current meant paying to retake a proctored test every 24 months; now it is free online recurrent training (course ALC-677) that also covers the 2021 night-operations and operations-over-people rules. The certificate itself never expires; only recency lapses, and a lapsed pilot simply completes the training before flying again.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - UAS requirements



Must weigh less than 55 lbs
Must be registered in FAADroneZone ($5, valid 3 years)
Must comply with Remote ID
Must undergo a pre-flight check by the remote pilot in command





Under Part 107 every aircraft is registered individually regardless of weight (the 250 g threshold applies only to recreational registration). At 55 lbs and above you leave Part 107 entirely and need an exemption or airworthiness certification. The pre-flight check requirement (107.49) is where checklists, battery inspection, and control-link verification live; this becomes routine in the flight-planning topic.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - location requirements


Class B/C/D and Class E surface areas: operations require an airspace authorization, normally obtained through LAANC
Class G (uncontrolled): may operate while following all other Part 107 rules, no authorization needed


Walk through the airspace classes on the figure from the top down: A (18,000 ft and above, irrelevant to sUAS), B around major hubs like Charlotte, C around mid-size towered airports like RDU, D around smaller towered airports, E controlled airspace that can extend to the surface, G uncontrolled. The practical question for every mission: is my site under controlled airspace that reaches the surface? If yes, get a LAANC authorization first.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
LAANC - airspace authorization
Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability



Automated, near-real-time FAA authorization for flights in controlled airspace, up to the altitude in the UAS Facility Maps
Available to both Part 107 and recreational flyers
Request through an FAA-approved service supplier app (e.g. Aloft, AutoPylot, Airspace Link)
Above facility-map altitudes or where LAANC is unavailable: apply via FAADroneZone





LAANC replaced the old call-the-tower and 5-mile-notification era: since 2018-2019 authorization is an app workflow that usually returns approval in seconds. Demo one supplier app live if possible, showing the UAS Facility Map grid around RDU: each grid cell shows the maximum altitude the FAA will auto-authorize, and zero-grid cells require a manual FAADroneZone application with longer lead time. This is the single most-used regulatory tool students will touch in practice.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Reading aeronautical charts


Line Pattern

Solid line - higher class (more restrictive)
Dashed line - lower class (less restrictive)

Line Color

Blue line - higher class (more restrictive)
Magenta line - lower class (less restrictive)

FAA course on airspace classification

This translates to:

Solid blue - class B, Solid magenta - class C
Dashed blue - class D, Dashed magenta - class E

Interactive charts: VFRMap, SkyVector


Chart reading is heavily tested on the Part 107 exam, so this slide maps directly to Assignment 1B question types. Suggest pulling up SkyVector on the Raleigh area and having students identify the RDU Class C shelves and the dashed magenta Class E surface areas nearby. Remind them that the sectional shows airspace; the UAS Facility Map shows what LAANC will authorize, and both are needed for mission planning.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - operating rules

Must fly at or below 400 feet above ground level (AGL), or within 400 feet of a structure if flying higher




Must not fly from a moving vehicle unless in a sparsely populated area
Must fly at or below 100 mph (87 knots)
Must yield right of way to manned aircraft





The 400-ft-of-a-structure allowance (107.51) exists for tower and building inspection: you may fly up to 400 ft above a structure’s top while within a 400 ft radius of it. For mapping work in this course, flight altitude is chosen for ground sampling distance and is normally 200-400 ft AGL, so the ceiling rarely binds, but it matters when a site sits under a low LAANC grid altitude.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - operating rules



Must keep the UAS within visual line of sight (VLOS) of the remote pilot in command or a visual observer
Night operations allowed without a waiver (since April 2021) if the pilot has completed current training and the aircraft has anti-collision lighting visible for 3 statute miles





VLOS means unaided eyes (glasses fine, binoculars or FPV goggles alone do not count); an FPV pilot needs a visual observer next to them. The 2021 rule ended the era of night waivers: before it, daylight-only operation (old 107.29) was the most-waived rule in Part 107. Thermal mapping missions, which fly at night or dawn for temperature contrast, are the course-relevant beneficiary.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Remote ID

UAS must broadcast identification, location, and control-station location during flight (rule effective 2021, enforced since March 16, 2024)
Three ways to comply:

Standard Remote ID aircraft (built-in broadcast)
Aircraft with an attached broadcast module (VLOS only)
Fly without Remote ID only inside an FAA-Recognized Identification Area (FRIA)

Applies to all aircraft that must be registered (recreational and Part 107)


Think of Remote ID as a digital license plate broadcast over WiFi/Bluetooth that anyone with a phone app can receive; the FAA and law enforcement can correlate it with registration data. FRIAs are fixed sites sponsored by CBOs and educational institutions, mostly model-aircraft fields. Practical note for the course: all recent DJI aircraft have standard Remote ID built in; check compliance for anything older or self-built.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Operations Over People - Categories 1-4
Since April 2021, routine flight over people is allowed under Part 107 if the aircraft qualifies for one of four categories (14 CFR Part 107 Subpart D).

Not to be confused with airspace classes B/C/D/E/G from earlier in this lecture
Category is a property of the aircraft (weight, injury severity, certification), not of the pilot
Sustained flight over open-air assemblies additionally requires Remote ID (Categories 1-3)


Set up the next four slides. Before 2021 any flight over a person outside your crew required a waiver; the Operations Over People rule made it routine, scaled to how much harm the aircraft could do. Emphasize the terminology trap: FAA “Category 1-4” (over-people) vs airspace “Class B-G”; the exam uses both. Also distinguish transiting over people (allowed per category) from sustained hovering over crowds.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Category 1
Eligibility: aircraft weighs 0.55 lb (250 g) or less, including everything attached.
Requirements:

No exposed rotating parts that could lacerate human skin
Remote ID required for sustained flight over open-air assemblies

Operations:

May fly over people without a waiver or a Declaration of Compliance

Example UAS: sub-250 g aircraft such as the DJI Mini series or DJI Neo (with propeller guards where needed to meet the laceration requirement)

Category 1 is self-declared: no FAA paperwork, the operator just has to be right about the weight and the laceration criterion. This is a major reason the sub-250 g market segment exists; manufacturers engineer to sit under the threshold. Weight includes payload, so adding a prop-guard set or beacon can push an aircraft out of Category 1.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Category 2 and Category 3
Eligibility: no weight limit; injury-severity based, demonstrated through an FAA-accepted Means of Compliance and a Declaration of Compliance by the manufacturer.

Category 2: impact must not exceed the severity of 11 ft-lbs of kinetic energy; no exposed lacerating parts; allows routine flight over people
Category 3: impact must not exceed 25 ft-lbs; no flight over open-air assemblies; over people only within a closed or restricted-access site with notice, or when people are under cover or in stationary vehicles


Categories 2 and 3 are manufacturer-certified, not operator-declared, and as of the mid-2020s very few aircraft hold accepted Declarations of Compliance, so these categories are rare in practice; most operators either stay in Category 1 or avoid flying over people entirely. The kinetic-energy thresholds translate to roughly a 2 lb and 4 lb aircraft at terminal velocity, though the tests are on impact severity, not weight.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Category 4
Eligibility: aircraft holds an airworthiness certificate issued under Part 21, like a crewed aircraft.
Requirements:

Operated within its approved flight manual limitations
Maintenance, inspection, and record-keeping program required

Operations:

May operate over people, including sustained flight over open-air assemblies, subject to the operating limitations in the certificate


Category 4 is the “certify it like an airplane” path, aimed at larger aircraft and future package-delivery style operations; it is out of reach for typical mapping platforms and no common survey drone uses it. For this course the takeaway hierarchy is: Category 1 if under 250 g, otherwise plan missions so you are not over people at all, which is standard practice for site mapping.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Waivers from Part 107 operating rules

To operate outside Part 107 rules, apply for a Certificate of Waiver through FAADroneZone
The FAA grants waivers when the proposed operation can be performed safely with the applicant’s proposed mitigations


The waiver process asks “how will you mitigate the risk this rule addresses?” and successful applications read like safety cases, not requests. Approval times run weeks to months, so waivers are planned mission infrastructure, not a quick fix. Since the 2021 rules absorbed night operations and some over-people flight, the dominant remaining waiver is beyond visual line of sight.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Waivable sections of Part 107



Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft (§ 107.25)
Visual line of sight aircraft operation (§ 107.31) - the most requested waiver today (BVLOS)
Visual observer (§ 107.33)
Operation of multiple small unmanned aircraft systems (§ 107.35)



Yielding the right of way (§ 107.37(a))
Operation over people (§ 107.39, beyond the category rules)
Operation in certain airspace (§ 107.41)
Operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft (§ 107.51)



No waiver will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire


BVLOS (107.31) waivers dominate because they unlock the economics of linear inspection, agriculture, and delivery: one pilot covering miles instead of a visual bubble. Daylight-only operation (old 107.29) used to top this list before the 2021 night rule removed the need. The carriage-for-hire exclusion is why drone delivery companies operate under separate exemptions and air-carrier rules, not Part 107 waivers.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Accident reporting (§ 107.9)
No later than 10 days after an operation, the remote pilot in command must report to the FAA any operation of the small unmanned aircraft involving at least:



Serious injury to any person or any loss of consciousness; or
Damage to any property, other than the small unmanned aircraft, unless the cost of repair (including materials and labor) or fair market value of the property does not exceed $500





Reports go through FAADroneZone. Note what does not trigger a report: destroying your own aircraft, or minor property damage under $500. “Serious injury” follows the AIS Level 3 standard, roughly an injury requiring hospitalization. Universities typically layer their own incident reporting on top, which connects to the NC State UAS procedures linked from the part page.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Where NOT to fly


Transition into airspace restrictions. The no-drone-zone signage is public outreach; the legal substance is in the TFRs, special-use airspace, and security restrictions on the following slides. Best pre-flight habit: check a LAANC/B4UFLY-service app the day of the flight, since restrictions appear and move (wildfires, VIP movement, sporting events).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Airspace restrictions



Security Sensitive Airspace Restrictions
Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs)
Restricted or Special Use Airspace
Stadiums and sporting events
Wildfires
Controlled airspace around airports (LAANC)





Preview the taxonomy: some restrictions are permanent and mapped (special use airspace, security areas), some are scheduled (stadium TFRs), some pop up with hours’ notice (wildfire TFRs). All of them override any LAANC authorization you may hold. The next slides take them one at a time.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Security Sensitive Airspace Restrictions



All UAS flights prohibited within the airspace
Restrictions extend from the ground up to 400 feet AGL
Apply to all types and purposes of UAS flight operations
Remain in effect 24 hours a day, 7 days a week



14 CFR § 99.7


These cover sites like military bases, national landmarks, and critical infrastructure designated at federal request. They are depicted on the FAA’s UAS-specific maps rather than sectionals, another reason to check a drone-specific app rather than only a pilot’s chart. Violations here draw federal attention quickly; some sites have counter-UAS authority.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Temporary Flight Restrictions



TFR: airspace where flight is limited because of a temporary hazardous condition (wildfire, chemical spill) or a security-related event (VIP movement, large public events)
The TFR text gives the details: size, altitude, effective times, and which operations are restricted or permitted




TFR map
TFR list



Presidential TFRs are the famous ones: a 30-nautical-mile ring that shuts down drone activity wherever the President travels, often on short notice. For fieldwork the operational lesson is to check TFRs the same day as the flight; a site that was clear during planning can be closed by a wildfire TFR the morning of the mission.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Restricted or Special Use Airspace


Types of Special Use Airspace include:

Prohibited areas
Restricted areas
Warning areas
Military operation areas (MOAs)
Alert areas
Controlled firing areas (CFAs)



The airspace surrounding Washington DC is the most restricted in the country More info


Prohibited areas (P-56 over the White House and National Mall) ban flight outright; restricted areas require permission from the using agency; MOAs and warning areas are legal but hazardous. North Carolina relevance: large MOAs and restricted areas sit east of Raleigh around Seymour Johnson AFB and the Dare County bombing range, which matters for coastal mapping projects.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Stadiums and sporting events


UAS operations are prohibited within a radius of 3 nautical miles of the stadium or venue, from one hour before to one hour after, for:

Major League Baseball
National Football League
NCAA Division One Football
NASCAR Cup Series, IndyCar, and Champ Series races





This is a standing TFR (FDC NOTAM 4/3621) up to 3,000 ft AGL. Local hook: Carter-Finley Stadium is on this list on football Saturdays, and the restriction covers a 3 nm radius, which reaches much of west Raleigh including parts of campus and Lake Wheeler Road. Check the game schedule before planning fall field days.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Wildfires


It is illegal to fly your UAS in or around a wildfire firefighting operation 




“If you fly, we can’t” is the fire community’s campaign line: a single drone sighting grounds firefighting aircraft. Wildfire TFRs carry civil penalties that can exceed $20,000 plus potential criminal liability. The legitimate path exists: public agencies fly fire-mapping missions under COAs in coordination with incident command, an application area from Lecture 1A.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Airports and controlled airspace

There is no “notify within 5 miles” rule anymore; that pre-2019 requirement was repealed with Section 336
Both recreational and Part 107 pilots need a LAANC (or FAADroneZone) authorization to fly in Class B, C, D, or surface Class E airspace
Authorization is granted up to the UAS Facility Map altitude for the grid cell; near runways this is often 0 ft (no automatic authorization)








Called out explicitly because the 5-mile rule persists in older videos and blog posts and in some exam-prep material. The current logic is airspace-based, not distance-based: a site 4 miles from an airport in Class G needs nothing, while a site 8 miles away under a Class C shelf that reaches the surface needs authorization. Always resolve the question with a facility-map app, not distance.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Public entities


Publicly funded universities, law enforcement agencies, fire departments, and other government agencies have two options:

Follow the same requirements and operating rules as commercial users (Part 107)

OR

Operate as public aircraft under a blanket Certificate of Authorization (COA)





In practice most public entities, including most university flight programs, simply use Part 107 because it is simpler and their missions fit within it; COAs are reserved for operations Part 107 cannot cover, such as certain law-enforcement or emergency operations. Ask the class why an agency might still want a COA (self-certification of pilots, emergency provisions, operations outside Part 107 limits).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Certificate of Authorization
Can be obtained:

Only by government entities, such as federal and state agencies, law enforcement, and public colleges and universities
Only for public (governmental) UAS aircraft operations

Allows:

Flights at or below 400 feet in Class G airspace nationwide
Self-certification of the UAS pilot
Emergency COAs under special circumstances


The blanket public COA is the standing nationwide authorization; operations outside it (higher altitudes, specific controlled airspace) need a jurisdictional COA for a defined area. Self-certification of pilots is the notable difference from Part 107: the agency, not the FAA, attests pilot qualification.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
section: How to apply for a COA?
text:
How to apply for a COA?

Applications are submitted online via the FAA’s COA process
Visit the FAA website for details on how to apply
The average COA processing time is less than 60 days
Expedited authorization is available in emergency and life-threatening situations
Sample COA Application


Mostly reference material; students will not file COAs themselves, but they may work under one. Emergency COAs matter after disasters: post-hurricane mapping flights in North Carolina have operated under expedited authorizations coordinated with emergency management, a direct link to the change-detection applications later in the course.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Educational use



Under 49 USC 44809(c) and FAA educational-user guidance, students at accredited institutions may fly under the recreational exception as part of coursework (TRUST, registration, and all other 44809 conditions still apply)
Faculty-directed research and flights that further university business generally require Part 107
In this course, instructional flight operations are conducted under Part 107 by certificated pilots


 


History for context: a May 2016 FAA legal interpretation first allowed student flying under model-aircraft rules; the 2018 Reauthorization Act wrote the concept into statute at 44809(c), and 2021 FAA guidance details when instructors and faculty can participate (limited assistance is fine; directing research flights is not recreational). The safe institutional default is Part 107 for anything tied to funded research.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
UAS best practices



If you can, tell other people you’ll be taking pictures or video of them before you do so
If someone has a reasonable expectation of privacy, don’t violate it by taking pictures or video, unless you’ve got a very good reason
Don’t fly over other people’s private property without permission if you can easily avoid doing so






These come from the NTIA voluntary best practices for UAS privacy: not law, but the professional norm, and often stricter than what the FAA requires. For mapping projects, landowner permission for takeoff, landing, and ground control points is both courteous and usually a practical necessity; the FAA governs the air, but the launch site is property law.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
UAS best practices



Don’t gather personal data for no reason, and don’t keep it for longer than you have to
If you keep sensitive data about other people, secure it against loss or theft
If someone asks you to delete personal data about him or her that you’ve gathered, do so, unless you’ve got a good reason not to




Don’t harass people with your drone




Data-handling practices map directly onto research-data management: orthophotos of residential areas contain personal data (faces, vehicles, backyards), and IRB or data-management plans may govern retention. Good habit to teach: plan flight lines to minimize capture of areas outside the study site rather than cropping afterwards.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Current developments - BVLOS and Part 108

The biggest open problem from earlier in this lecture: beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) flight without a waiver
The FAA published the proposed Part 108 rule (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, August 2025) to enable routine BVLOS operations
Built on automated traffic awareness/deconfliction services and aircraft airworthiness acceptance instead of one-off waivers
Expect the regulatory landscape to keep shifting; always check faa.gov/uas for current rules


Close the loop with the detect-and-avoid concern from the NAS slide: Part 108 is the FAA’s answer, replacing case-by-case BVLOS waivers with a performance-based rule using strategic deconfliction and third-party services. Check the current rulemaking status before lecture and update the class, since the final rule may land during or after this semester. Good discussion prompt: which mapping applications change most if BVLOS becomes routine? (Corridor mapping, large-area agriculture, disaster response.)

title: Assignment 2B
text:
Geoprocessing of the UAS data
Completing this assignment you will generate orthomosaic and Digital Surface Model using pictures taken from the UAS Trimble UX5 Rover (Flight mission executed on September 22nd 2016). The Study area is located at Lake Wheeler COA. Additionally you will be able to see the processing results in the generated report and optionally you will be able to export also 3D model and Point cloud as well as Camera calibration and orientation data.
The process can be very time consuming (depending on computational power of your device and desired quality). In order to minimize the processing time, we will process only fraction of the data collected and we will use imagery downsampled by 50%. It will allow us to generate outputs in the classroom.


General workflow (with GCPs)
Preparation

Stage 1: Building simple geometry (in order to place GCPs)
Stage 2: Placing GCPs
Stage 3: Building complex geometry
Stage 4: Exporting results



Preparation

Data

OPTION 1 - Small area
You can use a smaller area to accelerate processing. The photos are not downsampled in order to obtain the highest resolution of the outputs.

download data - photos, log and coordinates of 3 GCPs



OPTION 2: You can use your own data



Software

Agisoft Metashape Professional (installer)



Preferences
When launching Metashape for the first time, some settings need to be adjusted to optimize performance. These settings need to be done only once, at the first use of Metashape, and are loaded by default in subsequent sessions.

Menu > Tools > Preferences
General tab:

Leave default (optional – write log to file: enabled, if you want to save the txt log file)

GPU tab:

Check the USE CPU when performing GPU accelerated processing option at the bottom

Appearance Tab:

Leave default (or adjust to personal taste)

Navigation Tab:

Leave default (or adjust to personal taste)

Advanced tab:

Project Files

Keep key points: disabled
Keep depth maps: disabled
Store absolute image paths: disabled

Export/Import: enable all
Miscellaneous:

Enable fine level task division: enabled





Preferences






Stage 1: Aligning Photos
In order to localize the GCPs first a preliminary simple model needs to be built.

Adding photos

Menu > Workflow > Add Photos
Indicate the path to the folder (downloaded data) containing photos and select them all. In the Reference pane, you can see that the photos have been loaded, but the coordinate system indicates local coordinates. It can be changed in the Settings.
Click the settings icon  > change coordinate system to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326).







Note




Camera accuracy (m): Refers to the positional accuracy of camera geotags (lat/lon), typically 2.5–10 meters with standard GPS, or better with high-grade equipment.
Camera accuracy (deg): Relates to yaw, pitch, roll; set higher (e.g., 2°) if not measured precisely.
Marker accuracy (m): Indicates ground control point accuracy, usually 0.01–0.05 m, can specify x/y/z separately (e.g., 0.01/0.05).
Scale bar accuracy (m): Accuracy of measured distances between markers, often very precise (e.g., 0.001 m).
Marker accuracy (pixels): How precisely you can place a marker in an image; 0.1 px for targets, 0.5 px for natural features.
Keypoint accuracy (pixels): Weight for automatically detected points; typically 0.5–1 px due to variability in appearance.






Loading camera positions
Click Import button  on the Reference pane toolbar > select file containing camera positions information (2016_09_22_sample.txt) in the Open dialog.







Note



Agisoft supports the camera orientation files in 5 formats: .csv, .txt, .tel, .xml, and .log. The default format of the Trimble Aerial Imaging log is .jxl. In order to convert the Trimble .jxl log file please run script by Vaclav Petras or use provided already converted log in .txt format.


Make sure that the columns are named properly – you can adjust their placement by indicating column number (top right of dialog box).


Aligning photos

Accuracy: Low
Check: Reference preselection
Key point limit: default
Tie point limit: default
Adaptive camera model fitting: enabled


Menu > Workflow > Align Photos

Click Save  in the toolbar.




Stage 2: Placing GCPs

Loading the GCPs coordinates
Click Import button  on the Reference pane toolbar > select the file containing Ground Control Points (GCP_3.txt) coordinates in the Open dialog.

Make sure that the columns are named properly – you can adjust their placement by indicating column number (top right of dialog box). This time you uncheck the Rotation box since GCPs are stationary and do not need determining yaw pitch and roll angles.
The window with the message: Can’t find match for ‘UAV 3’ entry. Create new marker? will pop up.

Choose ‘Yes to All’ – it will create new marker for each of the named GCPs from the file. They will be listed in Reference pane under the list of photos.


Indicating GCPs on the pictures
Now you need to find each of the GCPs and indicate its localization on all photos depicting it. You can also see the process on the instructional video.
The Model pane shows approximate positions of GCPs, it is better visible if the ‘Show cameras’ option is disabled (Menu > View > Show/Hide Items > Show cameras).
 
Choose in the context menu of the selected point on the list (right click) > Filter Photos by Marker.

In the Photos pane appear only the images in which the currently selected GCP is probably* visible.






Note



*This is possible because our pictures are geotagged (log indicates the position of each photo), if you will be working with the pictures that are not geotagged or in the area that you don’t know and are not able to “guess” which photo depicts which GCP, it is useful to build the dense point cloud or even mesh and texture (see the following steps) to see the preliminary model of the area in the Model pane, not just a sparse cloud (this is depicted on the figures above).


Open an image by double clicking the thumbnail. It will open in a tab next to the Model pane. The GCP will appear as a grey icon . This icon needs to be moved to the middle of GCP visible on the photo.

Drag the marker to the correct measurement position. At that point, the marker will appear as a green flag, meaning it is enabled and will be used for further processing.
Double click on the next photo and repeat the steps. As soon as the GCP marker position has already been indicated on at least two images, the proposed position will almost exactly match the point of measurement. You can now slightly drag the marker to enable it (turning it into a green flag) or leave it unchanged (gray marker icon) to exclude it from processing.
Filter photos by each marker again. Agisoft adjusts the GCPs positions on the run, so you can locate the GCP on additional images that will appear in the Photos pane.
In this sample processing we will include 3 GCPs. Mathematically, you need to indicate marker positions for at least 3 GCPs. Accurate error estimates can be calculated with at least 4 GCPs, while often at least 5 are needed to cover the center of the project as well, which reduces the chance of error propagation and resulting terrain distortions especially on flat or undulating terrain types.
Click Save  in the toolbar.


Optimizing alignment
You can see the errors by clicking on the View Errors icon . Best results are obtained when the alignment is first optimized based on the camera coordinates only, and a second time based on the GCP only.
Click Optimize icon  in the Ground Control toolbar (check all the boxes).






Warning



Depending on the version of Metashap the optimize icon may appear as a star.




Optimizing based on the GCP Markers
In the Ground Control pane:

disable all the camera coordinates (select one > press Ctrl+A > right-click > choose Uncheck).
enable all the GCP Marker coordinates (select one > press Ctrl+A > right-click > choose Check).

Click Settings icon  in the Ground Control toolbar:

leave the default values (Marker accuracy (m) = 0.005 m)

Click Optimize icon  in the Ground Control toolbar (leave all options at the default).
Click Save  in the toolbar.
You can now see how much the errors were reduced through optimization by clicking on the View Errors icon .



Stage 3: Building complex geometry
Before starting the Build Dense Cloud step it is recommended to check the bounding box of the reconstruction (to make sure that it includes the whole region of interest, in all dimensions). The bounding box should also not be too large (increased processing time and memory requirements).
The bounding box can be adjusted using the Resize Region  and the Rotate Region  tool from the toolbar. Make sure that the base (red plane) is at the bottom.

The next steps will be time consuming (depending on the desired quality and number of pictures). You can execute them one step at the time or you can also set a batch processing that does not require user interaction until the end of geoprocessing (especially useful in case of Ultra High quality that requires even several days of processing). The batch processing will be explained at the end of this section.

Menu > Workflow > Build Dense Cloud (Build Point Cloud)

Quality: Medium
Depth filtering: Aggressive



Medium (will downsample the images to get a 3D coordinate every 4 pixels)
High (will downsample the images to get a 3D coordinate every 2 pixels; typically takes several hours but will give acceptable results for most cases)
Ultra high (will calculate a 3D coordinate for every pixel in original imagery; may take more than a day or several days)








Note



When working with large datasets take into consideration the RAM size requirements for the different target qualities with respect to the number of images (in appendix in the manual).



Click Save  in the toolbar


Menu > Workflow > Build Mesh (Build Model)

Source data: Dense cloud or Point cloud
Surface type: Height field
Face count: Medium
Advanced options: leave default







Note



Face count set at “0” means that Metashape will determine an optimum number of faces (but this may not be enough to describe all the features on terrain)





Menu > Workflow > Build Texture

Texture Type: Diffuse Map
Source Data: Images
Mapping mode: Orthophoto
Blending mode: Mosaic (default)
Texture size/count: 4096
Enable color correction: disabled (unchecked) (Not visible in all versions)

Click Save  in the toolbar



Editing geometry
Sometimes it is necessary to edit geometry before building texture atlas and exporting the model.
If the overlap of the original images was not sufficient, the model can contain holes. In this case, to obtain a holeless model, use the Close Holes command. It is crucial if you want to perform any volume calculations - in this case, 100% holes need to be closed.

Menu > Tools > Mesh (Model) > Close Holes
In the Close Holes dialog, select the size of the largest hole to be closed (in percentage of the total model size).






Warning



DO not choose 100% unless you are calculating volumes (then you have to close 100% holes)



This does not apply to our data, since we have sufficient image overlap. But due to strong dependency on weather conditions, the holes in data are common with UAS.



Building DEM

Menu > Workflow > Build DEM
In this step, the parameters of the exported DEM are determined. In order to work in the commonly used in NC reference system, we will not keep the project’s WGS84 system, but change it to NC State Plane (ESPG:3358).




Building Orthophoto

Menu > Workflow > Build Orthophoto (Orthomosaic)
Orthophoto can be built only in the same coordinate system as the DEM.




Batch processing

Menu > Workflow > Batch process > Add
Batch processing allows setting multiple processes in the preset order and executing them one after another without user intervention. All the parameters should be set the same as explained above.

Optimize Alignment (Align Photos) - if the GCPs were placed but the optimization not performed, otherwise: skip
Build Dense Cloud (Point cloud)
Build Mesh (Build Model)
Build Texture
Build DEM
Build Orthophoto (Build Orthomosaic)







Stage 4: Exporting results
This option will be disabled if you are working in the demo version.

Orthomosaic

File > Export Orthophoto > Export JPEG/TIFF/PNG

Projection Type: geographic (default)
Datum: WGS 1984
Write KML file (footprint) and World file (.tfw) = check if desired (if left unchecked, georeferencing information will still be contained in the GeoTIFF .tif file)
Blending mode: Mosaic (default)
Pixel size: leave default


Leave default values. Fill out the desired name and save as type TIFF/GeoTIFF (*.tif).

Menu > File > Export DEM

Leave default values. Fill out the desired name and save as type TIFF/GeoTIFF (*.tif).



Generating report

Menu > File > Generate report
Indicate the name and path for the PDF file.

Processing outputs from OPTION 1 (downsampled images) are provided here.

The following export steps are optional.



Model

Menu > File > Export model > OBJ/FBX/KMZ
Indicate the name, path, and format of the output model.
Metashape supports model export in the following formats: Wavefront OBJ, 3DS file format, VRML, COLLADA, Stanford PLY, STL models, Autodesk FBX, Autodesk DXF, Google Earth KMZ, U3D, Adobe PDF. Some file formats (OBJ, 3DS, VRML, COLLADA, PLY, FBX) save texture images in a separate file. The texture file should be kept in the same directory as the main file describing the geometry.
3D Models are a great visualization tool. Model generated by following the assignment instructions as well as model from full flight processing can be viewed on Sketchfab.

Menu > File > Export points

Metashape supports point cloud export in the following formats: Wavefront OBJ, Stanford PLY, XYZ text file format, ASPRS LAS, ASTM E57, U3D, Potree, Metashape OC3, PDF.

Indicate the name, path, and format of the output file.

title: Assignment 2B
Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Objectives

Understand how remote sensing & photogrammetry support geospatial data acquisition
Recognize aerial photo types and the measurement challenges they introduce
Explain why image processing (orthorectification) is needed for measurements
Grasp SfM concepts for creating 3D models from 2D images


These are the takeaways. We’ll move from fundamentals to workflow design.
Keep thinking about two questions: What do you want to measure? and What accuracy do you need?
Those answers determine flight planning, ground control, and processing parameters.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
What is Remote Sensing?

Sensing without contact: acquire data from a distance

Passive sensors: measure reflected/emitted energy (RGB, multispectral, thermal)

Active sensors: emit energy and measure returns (LiDAR, radar, sonar)


Remote sensing gives us information without touching the surface.
Drones typically carry passive RGB or multispectral cameras; LiDAR UAS are active sensors and directly measure range.
Keep this distinction in mind, SfM uses passive imagery but infers depth from parallax.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Photogrammetry (Why it matters)

3D coordinate measurement using photographs
Two broad modes: aerial vs terrestrial (close-range)
Historically crucial for mapping; now democratized via UAS


Photogrammetry is the science of turning photos into measurements.
With UAS, we’ve moved from expensive manned flights to frequent, targeted surveys, faster iteration, but also new pitfalls like rolling shutter and lens distortions we must correct.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Aerial Image Types

Vertical: camera nadir-pointing; lower perspective distortion; better for mapping
Oblique: camera tilted; richer façades/context; higher distortion; good for 3D


Vertical images are standard for map accuracy and uniform scale.
Obliques capture façades and undercuts but bring strong perspective effects, useful for 3D context and texture, less for planimetric measurements unless carefully modeled.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Why Raw Photos Mislead

Perspective projection (not orthographic)
Relief displacement: elevated features “lean” away from nadir
Lens and platform distortions (rolling shutter, radial/tangential lens errors)


If you try to measure distances on a raw photo, elevation and tilt cause scale to vary across the image.
Orthorectification corrects these effects so you can trust the geometry.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Orthorectification (What it does)

Removes perspective & relief distortion

Compensates optical distortions (camera model)

Produces a uniform-scale orthophoto suitable for measurement


Think of orthorectification as “unwarping” the image onto a known surface using camera parameters and elevation.
The output is metrically reliable, if the inputs and models are correct.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
What We Need (Inputs)

Digital imagery with sufficient overlap (≥70% forward, ≥60% side as a baseline)
DEM/DTM to remove relief distortion (or derive via SfM)
Exterior orientation (IMU/PPK/RTK or estimated in bundle adjustment)
Camera calibration (intrinsics: focal length, principal point, distortion)
Ground Control Points (GCPs) for georeferencing & accuracy assessment
Software implementing collinearity equations / bundle adjustment (SfM)


Overlap enables feature matching; more texture yields stronger geometry.
IMU/RTK help, but even with them, you’ll want checkpoints to validate accuracy.
Bundle adjustment simultaneously refines camera poses and 3D feature locations.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Geotagging (Limits & Use)

Embeds camera position in EXIF (approximate location/altitude)
Useful for initialization, not precision georeferencing
Expect meter-level errors without RTK/PPK or GCPs


Geotags get you in the right neighborhood.
For survey-grade outputs, you still need either high-quality GNSS (RTK/PPK) or well-placed GCPs and checkpoints to quantify accuracy.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Ground Control Points (GCPs)

Marked or photo-identifiable, stable, and well-distributed
Known X, Y, Z with survey-grade accuracy
Essential to improve precision and to validate results (use checkpoints)


Separate GCPs (to constrain the solution) from checkpoints (to evaluate it).
Distribute both across the project area, edges and varying elevations, to avoid biased solutions and inflated accuracy claims.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
From 2D Images to 3D (SfM)

Automated feature matching across overlapping images
Bundle adjustment estimates camera intrinsics/extrinsics + sparse 3D
Densification (stereo matching) → point cloud → mesh/DSM/orthophoto


SfM recovers relative 3D structure from parallax; scale and orientation come from geotags, RTK/PPK, or GCPs.
Quality hinges on image texture, overlap, camera model, and outlier handling.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Multiple-View Geometry (Intuition)

Correspondence: find the same feature in different views
Triangulation: intersect rays from multiple cameras → 3D point
Camera geometry: solve for poses that best explain all matches


Every matched pixel defines a ray in 3D; with two or more rays we triangulate a point.
The optimization balances all matches, minimizing reprojection error while refining camera parameters, this is the heart of SfM accuracy.

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
UAS Photogrammetric Workflow

Mission planning (GSD target, overlap, altitude, speed, lighting, safety)
Field ops (calibrated camera settings, consistent exposure, RTK/PPK optional)
Control survey (GCPs + checkpoints; stable, visible, distributed)
Processing (feature match → bundle adjust → densify)
Products (orthophoto, DSM/DTM, contours) + QA/QC (residuals, RMSE/NMAD)


Treat QA/QC as a product: report accuracy on independent checkpoints.
Inspect residuals, look for systematic tilt or doming, and check for artifacts on low-texture surfaces (water, uniform crops, snow).

title: Photogrammetry and Structure from Motion Concepts
text:
Common Pitfalls & Fixes

Low texture / repetitive patterns → add obliques; fly lower; diversify look angles
Rolling shutter → shorter exposure, slower speed, global shutter if possible
Doming / bowl surfaces → stronger control (GCPs/RTK), better geometry
Vegetation canopy bias → model as DSM; don’t compare to DTM
Shadowing/lighting changes → plan time of day; manual exposure


Most failures are geometric or radiometric: improve image geometry or stabilize exposure.
Always separate DSM vs DTM use-cases, don’t mistake canopy for ground.

title: Lab: Processing lidar and UAS SfM point clouds
text:
GIS-based analysis of point clouds
Launch GRASS GIS with the Lake_Wheeler_ncspm location. Create a new mapset for this assignment.
Change the current working directory to the directory where you downloaded the LAS files using cd command and path or in case you work in command line in GRASS GUI just type cd and press enter and select the directory using a dialog.
cd ~/Downloads
Let’s first look at the lidar point cloud metadata, particularly at the classes, we will later work with the classes 1 and 2.
Windows:
lasinfo mid_pines_spm_2013.las
Linux/Mac
pdal info mid_pines_spm_2013.las
The output shows number of points in each class:
  Point Classifications
---------------------------------------------------------
    1340658 Unclassified (1) 
    2580704 Ground (2) 
    66 Low Point (noise) (7) 
    1960603 Reserved for ASPRS Definition (11) 
Class 11 - for the explanation of Categories in this class refer to p. 10 in ASPRS LAS specification file. In this particular case, the classification scheme was not used - the metadata define class 11 as “withheld”.
Get the geographic extent of the point cloud and then set the computational region to tis extent:
r.in.lidar -sgo input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las
g.region n=220218 s=218694 e=637795 w=636271 -p

Explore the density of points

Lidar point cloud
First we set the resolution to 1 meter (flag -a ensures region boundaries are adjusted to be even multiples of the resolution value):
g.region res=1 -pa
Compute the density of all points using binning:
r.in.lidar -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_dens_all method=n
d.rast mid_pines_dens_all
d.legend -f -s -d rast=mid_pines_dens_all at=5,50,7,10
d.out.file mid_pines_dens_all.png
Compute the density of ground points and set histogram equalized color table for both densities so that we can compare them:
r.in.lidar -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_dens_ground class_filter=2 method=n
r.colors -e map=mid_pines_dens_all,mid_pines_dens_ground color=bcyr
d.rast mid_pines_dens_ground
Compare both rasters and save as images for report.
Later, we will examine the density using v.outlier and imported vector points.



Lidar point cloud: raster binning and classification
Compute different surfaces by binning. Explore what different returns and classes show.
Create a raster map of classes:

1 - ground
2 - vegetation
3 - buildings

Create DSM:
g.region n=220218 s=218694 e=637795 w=636271 res=2 -pa
r.in.lidar -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_all_max method=max resolution=3 class_filter=1,2
Create surface based on last return






Caution



Last return with r.in.lidar represents canopy because it filters last return where there are multiple returns.
In general, last return represents the overall last return from the lidar pulse an is commonly used to identify ground.


r.in.lidar -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_last_mean method=mean return_filter=last class_filter=1,2
Create surface representing ground based on already classified points:
r.in.lidar -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_ground_mean class_filter=2
Combine surfaces and create classes:

1 - ground
2 - vegetation
3 - buildings

r.mapcalc "classes = if( not(isnull(mid_pines_last_mean)), 2, if( not(isnull(mid_pines_ground_mean)), 1, if( not(isnull(mid_pines_all_max)), 3, null())))"
Set colors with r.colors (right click on classes layer - Set color table), copy and paste the following color rules into “or enter values directly” text field located in Define tab (option rules):
1 220:220:180
2 0:180:0
3 150:0:0
Look at places where our simplistic classification failed to properly identify buildings. Save image to file:
d.out.file classes.png


High resolution DEM/DSM
Import the point cloud as vector points (without attribute table, not necessary to build points):
v.in.lidar -b -t -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_ground class_filter=2
v.in.lidar -b -t -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_surface class_filter=1,2 return_filter=first
Remove the vector layers from your Layer Manager if they were added (you can disable automatic adding of layers in the dialog for the module).
Check the point overall point density using v.outlier:
v.outlier -e input=mid_pines_ground

Estimated point density: 1.111 Estimated mean distance between points: 0.9487

Interpolate with resolution 0.3 meter, also create slope and profile curvature map.
g.region n=219780 s=219100 e=637250 w=636575 res=0.5 -pa
v.surf.rst input=mid_pines_ground elevation=mid_pines_ground_elev slope=mid_pines_ground_slope pcurv=mid_pines_ground_profcurv npmin=80 tension=20 smooth=1
v.surf.rst input=mid_pines_surface elevation=mid_pines_surface_elev slope=mid_pines_surface_slope pcurv=mid_pines_surface_profcurv npmin=80 tension=20 smooth=1
r.colors map=mid_pines_ground_elev,mid_pines_surface_elev color=elevation
You can recompute it with higher npmin=150 to reduce artifacts from segmentation visible on slope and curvature maps (will be much slower!).
Visualize DEM and DSM in 3D view, use cross-sections.
Leave just raster map ‘mid_pines_surface_elev’ in Layer Manager, hide legend, zoom to computational region. Go to 3D view, set surface resolution 1 and color to map ‘classes’. Save images.


Compute the difference of lidar DEM and GCP heights
First, download the GCP_12_decimal pack file
and unpack it to GRASS
v.unpack GCP_12_decimal.pack
Then, add the columns:
v.db.addcolumn map=GCP_12_decimal columns="dem_height DOUBLE, height_difference DOUBLE"
Query (sample) the raster elevation at the locations of GCPs:
v.what.rast -i map=GCP_12_decimal raster=mid_pines_ground_elev column=dem_height
Compute the difference and save it in the attribute column:
v.db.update map=GCP_12_decimal column=height_difference query_column="ASL - dem_height"
View the results:
v.db.select map=GCP_12_decimal columns=ASL,dem_height,height_difference
Compute extended univariate statistics and show thematic map:
v.univar -e GCP_12_decimal column=height_difference
d.vect.thematic map=GCP_12_decimal column=height_difference algorithm=int nclasses=4 colors=blue,30:144:255,173:216:230,255:192:203 icon=basic/circle size=20
d.legend.vect at=10,40
Alternatively use Attribute Table Manager to view the results.


Ground classification (optional)
Download extension v.lidar.mcc:
g.extension v.lidar.mcc
Module v.lidar.mcc uses a multiscale curvature-based classification algorithm to distinguish ground and non-ground points:
g.region n=219511 s=219354 w=637071 e=637249 res=1
v.in.lidar -t -r -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_sample
v.lidar.mcc input=mid_pines_sample ground=ground nonground=nonground
Visualize classification results in 2D or 3D.



Visualize point density in 3D (optional)
Convert LAS file into text file:
las2txt -i mid_pines_spm_2013.las --parse xyzc -o mid_pines.txt
Set smaller region for creating the 3D raster:
g.region n=219502 s=219348 w=637070 e=637276 b=110 t=135 res=2 res3=2 tbres=0.5 -p3
Use binning to create point density 3D raster. Run r3.in.lidar, directly on the LAS file:
r3.in.lidar -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las n=mid_pines_dens
With older GRASS versions where r3.in.lidar was not available yet use an alternative tool:
r3.in.xyz input=mid_pines.txt output=mid_pines_dens method=n separator=comma
Set custom color table with r3.colors:
0% 255:255:100
5% green
100% red
Visualize point density in 3D view using slices and isosurfaces:

Leave only 3D raster mid_pines_dens in Layer Manager.
Set computational region based on the 3D raster and zoom to it.
Switch to 3D.
On View page press Reset, set Height to 50 and Z-exag to 2. Nothing is visible yet.
On Data page - 3D raster, check Draw wire box, set resolution to 1.
Add isosurface and set isosurface value 1 and press Enter.
Check toggle normal direction and set different color of isosurface.
Experiment with different isosurface levels (press enter to confirm the new value).
Remove isosurface, change draw mode to slices, add slice and set its axis to Z.
Manipulate with the slice.
Save images for report.




Lidar transect visualization (optional)
Download extension v.profile.points:
g.extension v.profile.points
We will import small sample of lidar points (limited by computational region extent) with attribute table:
g.region n=219452 s=219450 w=637132 e=637134
v.in.lidar -r -o input=mid_pines_spm_2013.las output=mid_pines_all
Compute profile, set the color based on intensity values in attribute table, and visualize. You need to zoom to the vector map to see it:
v.profile.points point_input=mid_pines_all output=profile width=5 coordinates=637106,219373,637132,219451
v.colors map=profile use=attr column=intensity color=grass
d.vect map=profile color=none width=1 icon=basic/circle


UAS point cloud density (optional)
Note: importing this UAV point cloud may not work for you on Windows.
Import binned UAV for subarea. First find the extent, then set the region:
r.in.lidar -go input=2015_06_sample_points_NCspm.las out=midpines_uav_06_02m_raw
g.region n=219660 s=219288 e=637287 w=636876 res=1 -pa
Compute the point density at 1 meter resolution and compare with previously computed lidar point density:
r.in.lidar -o input=2015_06_sample_points_NCspm.las out=midpines_uav_06_1m_dens method=n
r.colors -e map=mid_pines_dens_all,mid_pines_dens_ground,midpines_uav_06_1m_dens color=bcyr
Add legend of the UAV density:
d.legend -f -s -d rast=midpines_uav_06_1m_dens at=5,50,7,10
Zoom to the UAS subarea and compare the lidar and UAS densities, save images.

title: Assignment 5B
section: Analyze time series of UAS DSMs
text:
Analyze time series of UAS DSMs

Create a new mapset and copy the UAS DSMs
Start GRASS in Lake_Wheeler_NCspm project and create a new mapset. Open GRASS in this mapset
g.copy raster=2015_03_18_DSM_agi_6GCP@PERMANENT,2015_03_18_DSM_agi_6GCP
g.copy raster=2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP@PERMANENT,2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP
g.copy raster=2015_07_27_DSM_agi_2GCP_4ID@PERMANENT,2015_07_27_DSM_agi_2GCP_4ID 
g.copy raster=2015_08_14_DSM_agi_3GCP_4ID@PERMANENT,2015_08_14_DSM_agi_3GCP_4ID 
g.copy raster=2015_09_04_DSM_agi_6GCP@PERMANENT,2015_09_04_DSM_agi_6GCP
g.copy raster=2015_09_21_DSM_agi_6GCP@PERMANENT,2015_09_21_DSM_agi_6GCP
g.copy raster=2015_10_06_DSM_agi_8GCPs@PERMANENT,2015_10_06_DSM_agi_8GCPs


Register the time series in temporal framework
First, create a space-time raster dataset (STRDS) with absolute temporal type:
t.create output=uas_dsm type=strds temporaltype=absolute semantictype=mean title="UAS_DSM" description="UAS-based 2015 DSMs processed by Agisoft"
Now, create a text file named “series.txt” with the following content in your working directory, or download the prepared file into your working directory.
These are the DSMs with their time stamps:
2015_03_18_DSM_agi_6GCP|2015-03-18
2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP|2015-06-20
2015_07_27_DSM_agi_2GCP_4ID|2015-07-27
2015_08_14_DSM_agi_3GCP_4ID|2015-08-14
2015_09_04_DSM_agi_6GCP|2015-09-04
2015_09_21_DSM_agi_6GCP|2015-09-21
2015_10_06_DSM_agi_8GCPs|2015-10-06
Register the DSMs into the created STRDS uas_dsm:
t.register input=uas_dsm file=series.txt
Now check it was registered correctly:
t.info input=uas_dsm
See different ways we can list raster maps registered in the dataset:
t.rast.list input=uas_dsm columns=name,start_time where="start_time >= '2015-08-01'"
t.rast.list input=uas_dsm columns=name,start_time,min,max
Verify the listed raster maps are actually in the database:
g.list type=raster pattern="2015*"
You can also use the Data tab in Layer Manager.
We can set common color table to all maps in the dataset:
t.rast.colors input=uas_dsm color=elevation
d.rast 2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP
d.rast 2015_10_06_DSM_agi_8GCPs
To get better idea about the dates and spatial extents, we can use Timeline tool accessible from Temporal - GUI tools - Timeline tool.
Select dataset uas_dsm, you can click on the drawn data points, and then also check 3D plot of spatio-temporal extents. Stretch the window as needed.
We can plot the elevation timeseries using Temporal Plot Tool.

Open the tool from Temporal - GUI tools - Temporal plot tool.
Select dataset uas_dsm and click on the arrow next to the X and Y coordinates field.
Then click somewhere on the Map Display and press Draw.

You should see a plot of elevation values. Try different places (road, field, building).


Find the area mapped by all surveys
We will find area mapped by all surveys. First we will set the extent to the maximum bounding box, use t.info to get the values:
t.info input=uas_dsm -g
g.region n=219942 s=219037 e=637439 w=636456 -pa res=0.3
Next, we use t.rast.series to derive raster representing the number of overlapping DSMs. By using -n flag we create masking raster representing the intersection of all DSMs, and then we change computational region to the extent of its non-null bounding box:
t.rast.series input=uas_dsm method=count output=count
t.rast.series input=uas_dsm method=count output=intersection -n
d.rast count
d.rast intersection
g.region zoom=intersection -p
r.mask raster=intersection






TipQuestion



How large is the area? (use r.report)




Temporal aggregation
Our space-time raster dataset contains two DSMs from September:
t.rast.list input=uas_dsm columns=name,start_time
We will temporally aggregate the dataset by month by averaging all DSMs within each month (in this case averaging the September DSMs):
t.rast.aggregate input=uas_dsm output=uas_dsm_aggr basename=uas_dsm_aggr suffix=time granularity="1 months" method=average
t.rast.list input=uas_dsm_aggr columns=name,start_time


Minimum elevation (core)
You should already have lidar DSM and DEMs if you haven’t done already, unzip it in your working directory and unpack:
r.unpack -o input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm.pack
r.unpack -o input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dem.pack






TipQuestion



Find the minimum elevation (core) - how close it is to lidar bare ground?


t.rast.series input=uas_dsm method=minimum output=minimum
r.mapcalc "diff_lidar_uas = mid_pines_lidar2013_dem - minimum"
r.colors map=diff_lidar_uas color=differences
d.rast diff_lidar_uas
Parts of the minimum raster are significantly below lidar ground, find out which DSM is causing it:
t.rast.series input=uas_dsm method=min_raster output=min_raster
d.rast min_raster
Display resulting raster min_raster and query it (select the layer in Layer Manager and use Query tool in Map Display) or use r.what:
r.what map=min_raster coordinates=636879,219432
r.what map=min_raster coordinates=637232,219651
Value 2 represents third (numbering starts with 0) raster in our time series. Since there is some problem with the third and fourth raster (2015_07_27_DSM_agi_2GCP_4ID, 2015_08_14_DSM_agi_3GCP_4ID), we will exclude them from the analysis:
t.rast.series input=uas_dsm method=minimum output=minimum where="start_time < '2015-07-01' or start_time > '2015-09-01'" --o
r.mapcalc "diff_lidar_uas = mid_pines_lidar2013_dem - minimum" --o
r.colors map=diff_lidar_uas color=differences
Apply now the color table dif_lidar_uav.txt we used for highlighting differences in the last assignment:
 -40 red
 -1 orange
 -0.5 yellow
 -0.1 grey
 0 white
 0.1 grey
 0.5 cyan
 1 aqua
 40 blue
r.colors map=diff_lidar_uas rules=dif_lidar_uav.txt






TipQuestion



Explain what you see.


Let’s look now which temporal datasets we have:
t.list columns=id,number_of_maps,start_time

text:
Estimate crop biomass
We will use raster algebra on the time series to compute crop biomass. First we need to make sure that we take into account only fields (not forests).
You can use get the packed raster representation of fields (link is at the top).
We assume crop is anything higher than 0.3 and lower than 2 m (to exclude the building for example):
r.unpack -o fields.pack
t.rast.mapcalc inputs=uas_dsm expression="if (fields, if(uas_dsm - mid_pines_lidar2013_dem > 0.3 && uas_dsm - mid_pines_lidar2013_dem < 2, uas_dsm - mid_pines_lidar2013_dem, null()))" output=veg_uas_lidar basename=veg_uas_lidar
t.rast.univar input=veg_uas_lidar where="start_time < '2015-07-01' or start_time > '2015-09-01'"
d.rast veg_uas_lidar_2
r.report -n map=veg_uas_lidar_2 units=me nsteps=1
r.univar map=veg_uas_lidar_2
Use Python shell (tab in Layer Manager) to compute the biomass volume for June (paste each line into Python shell and press Enter):
sum = gs.parse_command('r.univar', map='veg_uas_lidar_2', flags='g')['sum']
float(sum) * gs.region()['nsres'] * gs.region()['ewres']
Remove the mask before we proceed in further analysis:
r.mask -r

title: Assignment 5B
section: Evaluate impact of vegetation change on viewshed extent
text:
Evaluate impact of vegetation change on viewshed extent
We would like to set up a webcam to monitor this area. First we will compute a cumulative viewshed of this area to find places from which we will have likely good visibility. We pick several places distributed all over the area from which we compute viewsheds on a lidar DSM with observer height of 3 meters (webcam height).
g.region raster=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm res=1 -pa
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=vshed_1 coordinates=637087,219376 observer_elevation=3
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=vshed_2 coordinates=637004,219653 observer_elevation=3
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=vshed_3 coordinates=636782,219374 observer_elevation=3
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=vshed_4 coordinates=636839,219150 observer_elevation=3
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=vshed_5 coordinates=636665,219527 observer_elevation=3
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=vshed_6 coordinates=636863,219503 observer_elevation=3
Now we compute the cumulative viewshed as the number of places (from the coordinates above) from which a cell is visible. This gives us better idea which places are visually more prominent and therefore likely to have good view of the fields.
r.series input=vshed_1,vshed_2,vshed_3,vshed_4,vshed_5,vshed_6 output=cum_viewshed method=count
d.rast cum_viewshed
Display the result with legend to see which places are potentially good for placing a webcam.
Since we need the webcam to capture the field during entire year we can run t.rast.series with method=maximum on the time series of UAS DSMs to derive the DSM series envelope surface and use it to analyze the viewshed. Of course, this assumes that the crops will be the same the following year. We exclude the problematic DSMs as we did while deriving the core surface:
g.region raster=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm
t.rast.series input=uas_dsm method=maximum output=maximum where="start_time < '2015-07-01' or start_time > '2015-09-01'"
We need to update the lidar-based DSM with the UAS envelope data and analyze the viewshed while taking into account the corn growing in the field. First we need to make sure that we take into account entire field to create a lidar-based DSM updated in the fields using UAS data.
r.mapcalc "maximum_clip = if (fields, maximum)"
r.patch.smooth input_a=maximum_clip input_b=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=lidar_maximum_dsm smooth_dist=10
r.relief lidar_maximum_dsm out=lidar_maximum_dsm_relief zscale=5
d.rast lidar_maximum_dsm_relief






TipQuestion



Look at the relief map around the building - where do people park their cars?


Now we selected a location based on the cumulative viewshed and look at the difference between the viewshed based on lidar and the envelope surface:
r.viewshed input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm output=viewshed_lidar_dsm observer_elevation=3 coordinates=636917,219223
r.viewshed input=lidar_maximum_dsm output=viewshed_maximum observer_elevation=3 coordinates=636917,219223

r.colors viewshed_lidar_dsm co=reds
r.colors viewshed_maximum co=greens
To compare the viewsheds display the resulting maps with transparency.






TipQuestion



Discuss the result. Can you find a better place for the webcam? Would placing the webcam higher help?



Estimate volume of a building
We need to first extract the mask of the building:
g.region n=219388.5 s=219366.9 w=637100.1 e=637138.5 res=0.3 -pa
r.mapcalc "building = 2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP - mid_pines_lidar2013_dem"
r.mapcalc "building_mask = if(building > 2, 1, null())"
Now we compute the volume
r.volume input=building clump=building_mask

Fusion Method
Linear combination of elevation surfaces \(z_{A}\) and \(z_{B}\) with weights given by overlap width \(s\) and distance \(d\) to the edge of \(z_{A}\):


\[
z_{AB} = z_{A} w + z_{B}(1 - w),
\\[10pt]
w = f(s, d) =
\begin{cases}
  \frac{d}{s} & 0 \leq d < s \\
  1 & d \geq s
\end{cases}
\]
